lead: The IPv4 datagram is the basic unit that carries data across the Internet. Its header contains fields that identify the source, destination, length and how the packet should be treated. When a link cannot carry the whole datagram because its Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) is smaller, the datagram is split into fragments. Each fragment is sent separately and later reassembled at the destination. Understanding the format, MTU limits and fragmentation rules is essential for designing reliable network applications and for troubleshooting packet loss.

blocks.text: An IPv4 datagram begins with a 20‑byte header. The first byte holds the Version (always 4) and the Internet Header Length (IHL) which tells how many 32‑bit words the header occupies. The Total Length field gives the size of the whole datagram in bytes, including header and data. Identification is a 16‑bit number that stays the same for all fragments of the same original packet.

The Flags field has three bits; the most important are DF (Don’t Fragment) and MF (More Fragments). The Fragment Offset field stores the start of the fragment in units of 8 bytes. TTL (Time‑to‑Live) limits how many hops the datagram may travel. Protocol indicates the next‑layer protocol (e.g., 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP). Header Checksum protects the header from corruption. Finally, the Source and Destination fields contain 32‑bit IPv4 addresses.

items: Version/IHL – 4 bits each
Total Length – 16 bits, bytes
Identification – 16 bits, same for all fragments
Flags – DF, MF, Reserved
Fragment Offset – 13 bits, 8‑byte units
TTL – 8 bits, hop count
Protocol – 8 bits, next‑layer ID
Header Checksum – 16 bits
Source / Destination – 32 bits each

blocks.text: Every physical link defines a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU). The MTU is the largest packet size, header included, that can be transmitted without breaking the frame. If an IPv4 datagram’s Total Length exceeds the MTU of the outgoing link, the router must fragment the datagram unless the DF flag is set.

items: Subtract the IPv4 header size (usually 20 bytes) from the MTU to obtain the maximum data payload per fragment.
Divide the payload into chunks that are multiples of 8 bytes, because the Fragment Offset is measured in 8‑byte units.

Create a new header for each fragment. Copy all fields from the original header, but set the Identification to the original value, set the MF flag to 1 for all fragments except the last, and compute the correct Fragment Offset.
Re‑calculate the Header Checksum for each fragment.

blocks.where: bytes already sent – sum of payload bytes in previous fragments; Offset is stored in the 13‑bit Fragment Offset field

items: All fragments must arrive at the destination for reassembly; missing fragments cause the whole packet to be discarded.
Fragments may follow different paths and arrive out of order.
The original header’s options (if any) are copied only into the first fragment.
All fragments except the last must have a payload length that is a multiple of 8 bytes; the final fragment may be shorter.

blocks.text: The receiving host collects fragments that share the same Identification, Source and Destination addresses. It uses the Fragment Offset to place each payload segment at the correct position in a buffer. The MF flag tells whether more fragments are expected. When a fragment with MF = 0 arrives and all earlier offsets are present, the host assembles the complete datagram and passes it to the next layer.

items: Create a reassembly buffer sized to the total length indicated by the fragment that has MF = 0 (the last fragment), or compute the required size as (Fragment Offset × 8) + payload length of that fragment.
Insert each fragment’s payload at (Fragment Offset × 8) bytes from the start of the buffer.
Mark the range as received. When the MF = 0 fragment arrives, note the final length.
If all byte ranges are marked, deliver the reassembled packet upward.

blocks.text: If any fragment is missing after a timeout (typically 60 seconds), the host discards the incomplete packet and may send an ICMP Time Exceeded – Fragment Reassembly Time Exceeded (Type 11, Code 1) message to the source.

examples.question: An IP packet of 3000 bytes (including the 20‑byte header) must travel over a link whose MTU is 1500 bytes. The source address is 192.168.1.10 and the destination address is 203.0.113.5. Show how the router fragments the packet. List for each fragment: Total Length, Payload bytes, Fragment Offset (in 8‑byte units), and MF flag.
steps: Maximum data per fragment = MTU – header = 1500 – 20 = 1480 bytes.
Fragment 1: payload = 1480 bytes, Total Length = 1480 + 20 = 1500 bytes, Offset = 0, MF = 1.
Fragment 2: payload = 1480 bytes, Total Length = 1500 bytes, Offset = (1480 ÷ 8) = 185, MF = 1.
Fragment 3: payload = 20 bytes, Total Length = 20 + 20 = 40 bytes, Offset = ((1480 + 1480) ÷ 8) = 370, MF = 0.
examples.answer: The packet is split into three fragments: (1) Length 1500 bytes, Offset 0, MF = 1; (2) Length 1500 bytes, Offset 185, MF = 1; (3) Length 40 bytes, Offset 370, MF = 0.
examples.check:
payload = 2980
mtu = 1500
header = 20
max_data = mtu - header
offsets = []
lengths = []
remaining = payload
while remaining > 0:
    data = min(max_data, remaining)
    total = data + header
    offset = (payload - remaining) // 8
    mf = 1 if remaining - data > 0 else 0
    lengths.append(total)
    offsets.append(offset)
    remaining -= data
print('Lengths:', lengths)
print('Offsets:', offsets)
print('MF flags:', [1 if o != offsets[-1] else 0 for o in offsets])

traps: Using a byte offset directly in the Fragment Offset field instead of dividing by 8; the field stores 8‑byte units.
Assuming the DF (Don’t Fragment) flag is always cleared; if DF=1 the router must drop the packet and send an ICMP Destination Unreachable.
Adding the header size to each fragment’s payload again, which would double‑count the header and produce a total length larger than the MTU.
Fragmenting a packet whose payload size is not a multiple of 8 bytes and forgetting to make the last fragment’s payload a multiple of 8 bytes (except the final fragment).

quiz.q: What is the size of the IPv4 header without options?
Explain why the Fragment Offset field is measured in 8‑byte units.
quiz.a: The offset is stored in a 13‑bit field. Measuring in 8‑byte units allows the offset to represent up to 8191 × 8 = 65 528 bytes. The final fragment can add up to 7 more bytes, so the maximum IPv4 datagram size is 65 535 bytes.

quiz.q: A router receives a 4000‑byte IPv4 packet (including header) on a link with MTU 1300 bytes. The DF flag is cleared. Determine the number of fragments and the Total Length of each fragment.
quiz.a: Maximum data per fragment = 1300 – 20 = 1280 bytes. Payload = 3980 bytes. Fragments: 1) data 1280, length 1300; 2) data 1280, length 1300; 3) data 1280, length 1300; 4) remaining data 140, length 160. Four fragments are created.

quiz.q: Compute the Fragment Offset value (in the field) for the third fragment in the previous question.
quiz.a: Offset = (1280 + 1280) ÷ 8 = 2560 ÷ 8 = 320. The field stores the value 320.

quiz.q: A host receives two fragments of an IPv4 packet: Fragment A with Offset 0, Length 1500, MF = 1; Fragment B with Offset 185, Length 1500, MF = 0. Is the packet complete? Explain.
quiz.a: The two fragments cover payload bytes 0‑1479 and 1480‑2959 with no gap. Since the second fragment has MF = 0, it is the last fragment, and the combined payload length matches the original datagram. Therefore the packet is complete.

quiz.q: What action does a router take when it must forward a packet larger than the outgoing MTU and the DF flag is set?
quiz.a: The router discards the packet and sends an ICMP Destination Unreachable – Fragmentation Needed message to the source.

quiz.q: Which IPv4 header field indicates the protocol of the encapsulated payload?

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern data‑center networks, hardware offloads perform fragmentation and reassembly to reduce CPU load. Research on Path MTU Discovery aims to avoid fragmentation by learning the smallest MTU along a route. IPv6 removes the header checksum and makes fragmentation the responsibility of the source, encouraging end‑to‑end MTU awareness. Future curricula often combine IPv4 fragmentation with security topics, such as how overlapping fragments can be used in evasion attacks.
